chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 241 to 260: short akam poems in which the body and the land are read as evidence: eyes that weep or block a chariot (241, 256), a forehead restored by a look at his hill (249), shoulders that swell as an omen (260), peacocks and stags that misread or mark the season (250, 251), and the mother's watch and the town's talk that hem the lovers in (244, 246, 248, 257).

241.reading: The woman tells her friend that while she herself bears her love, her eyes, out of their own intimacy with him, have wept: the eyes that saw the man of the hill country, where the small-headed boys who have herded the calves home raise a guarding shout at the vengai blooming in the village common, without climbing it, and the shout echoes in the sky-touching clefts.
241.nuance: She splits herself: she bears the desire in silence and the eyes break down. கெழுதகைமை is the closeness of old intimates, so the eyes weep out of their own bond with the man they saw, not on her orders. The boys' shout at the flowering vengai is the cry raised to bring its flowers down without climbing; the vengai's bloom also marks the millet harvest and the time for marriage, but the poem does not draw that out, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill, its vengai and its herd boys place the love in the kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; தோழி in line 2 names the addressee

242.reading: The foster mother says the girl lives in a small village in the flower-scented scrub, where the jungle cock with its calling voice, cool drops dripping from its bright-spotted neck, sweeps the water off the bushes; and even when the young lord goes to another town on work the king sends, his chariot does not know how to stay the night away.
242.nuance: The proof of the marriage is negative: the chariot does not know how to stay away. The king's business, which elsewhere takes a husband away for whole seasons, cannot keep this one for a night. The wet cock of the rainy scrub sets the season of waiting that this household is spared, which is why the mullai uri is here only to be denied.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-wet scrub and its jungle cock set the mullai household

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the foster mother reports on the wedded daughter; the poem names no addressee

243.reading: The woman says she will not think of the lord of the great sea shore where birds cry, where girls with bright bangles play at sand houses after plucking the bright flowers, like the bells on a garland, of the adumbu whose forked leaves are like a deer's hoofprint: let my eyes sleep, friend.
243.nuance: The vow not to think is made so that the eyes may sleep, which concedes that thinking of him is what has kept them open. The girls at their sand houses are the play she has left behind, and she places them on his shore.

thinai_evidence.note: the adumbu and the sea shore are neythal, and she laments alone

comparisons.tenor: the forked leaf of the adumbu

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; தோழி in line 5 names the addressee

244.reading: The friend tells the man that they are not people who failed to hear him, in the dense midnight when everyone sleeps, trying the door at night like a strong elephant: they heard, lord, but like a fine peacock caught in a net, its crest ruffled and its plumes drooping, we lay held, because the unfair mother embraces us each time we stir.
244.nuance: The mother's embrace, the sign of her love, is the trap: அறனில் யாய், the mother without fairness, holds the girl closest exactly when she would rise. The friend answers the man's force (the elephant at the door) with the girl's helplessness (the netted peacock, crest and plumes spoiled, as her beauty will be by the wait).

thinai_evidence.note: the midnight tryst at the door is kurinji union

comparisons.tenor: the man pushing at the door
the girl held fast in her mother's embrace

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; பெரும in line 3 names the man

245.reading: The woman says that worse than the loss of her beauty, which her companions in the seaside grove admired, would be for the unkindness of the lord of the soft shore, where the screw-pine with lush, sword-edged spathes stands as a fence like spears planted in a row, to spread wide and come out for many to know.
245.nuance: She ranks two losses and chooses the private one: her wasted beauty she can bear, the public knowledge of his unkindness she cannot, since it shames them both and closes the way to marriage. His shore is one where even the screw-pine stands armed as a fence, yet he guards nothing of hers; that is a single correspondence, so it is not tagged as ullurai. Whether மாலை in line 4 is a row (of spears) or evening, and how ஆய மாய்ந்த in line 1 divides, are not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the screw-pine shore is neythal and she laments

comparisons.tenor: the edges of the screw-pine spathes

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

246.reading: The woman says that because people say a chariot came and turned back at midnight for one who was alone, when the small white crow of the great sea's shore, stirring the green leaves broad as an elephant's ear, searches the cold backwater, her mother torments her; yet there are other girls, young and simple, with braided hair and bright jewels, the lucky ones, whose mothers do not torment them.
246.nuance: The rumour is true and the punishment falls on her alone, and she complains to fate: நற்பாலோர், those of good portion, are not better girls but girls with gentler mothers. The crow searching the cold backwater is awake at the hour the chariot came; it is witness and setting, and does nothing a person of the situation does, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the crow of the backwater sets the shore, and she laments

comparisons.tenor: the broad green leaves of the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

247.reading: The friend says she knew then that the flawless friendship from the chest of the man of the country, where the vengai sheds blossom from its soft unwithering branches and the elephant's deep sleep is heard, has great beauty, comes to sweet fruit, is righteous like the work of the able, and is a raft for people with kin.
247.nuance: A secret love is praised in the language of public virtue, beauty, fruit, righteousness and a raft for the kin, so the friend presents it as an alliance fit for families. The elephant asleep under the flower-shedding vengai is the hill at rest; it does nothing a person of the situation does, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai and the sleeping elephant are of the hill

comparisons.tenor: the man's friendship, which carries the kin across

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives the friend as speaker; she addresses the heroine as தோழி in line 4

248.reading: The friend says the talk was sure to come: from the day he said 'embrace my chest' it has been drawing near and now it is here, friend; and the mother has learned of it, from those telling big things about the lord of the shore where the sand dune climbed by adumbu, which the west wind heaped up to bury the swaying trunks, makes the tall palmyras short.
248.nuance: The landscape inverts measure: the wind's sand makes tall palms short, and the town's talk makes the affair big (பெரிய கூறி against குறிய ஆகும்). That is one correspondence of size, and it is not clear what the buried palm stands for, so it is recorded here and not tagged as ullurai. Lines 1 and 2 are compressed, and what அது refers to, the talk or his coming, is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the dune, the adumbu and the palmyra are of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; தோழி in line 3 names the addressee

249.reading: The woman tells her friend that she looked toward the hills of his country, whose slopes the heavy rain has drenched, making the grey-faced langur shiver with its young, in the thick-treed forest where flocks of peacocks call: see her forehead, is it not as it was before?
249.nuance: The cure is only a look at his hills from afar, and it works on her body at once: the forehead that had paled is as it was. The land she looks at is cold and wet, the langur and its young shivering in it; the pair does nothing a person of the situation does, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: his rain-soaked hill with its peacocks and langurs is kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; தோழி in line 4 names the addressee

250.reading: The man tells his charioteer to drive the wind-swift horses before evening comes, when the fine stag with its mate, having drunk the water in the pebbled hollow, frisks at the foot of the path: for the woman of painted eyes that rival the fighting carp of deep water, and of sweet, chosen words, is in bewildered distress.
250.nuance: He races the evening because evening is her worst hour; the stag with its mate is already where he wants to be. The colophon's paalai is the journey; the poem itself is the return, which is mullai's.

thinai_evidence.note: the man hurries home by evening to the waiting wife, the mullai situation

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the charioteer, called பாக in line 4; the colophon gives only the speaker

iraicchi.act: the stag, having drunk, frisks at evening together with its mate
iraicchi.sense: the man who sees the pair together presses to reach his own wife before the evening she spends alone

251.reading: The friend says the dark flocks of peacocks are foolish, bless them: thinking the season's rain had fallen, they danced to meet it, and the pidavam too has blossomed; but this is not the rainy season, friend, so let your grief end; they did it on hearing the thunder of a stray cloud that pours out the old water left from the rain that has passed so as to take in new.
251.nuance: The friend overturns the evidence the heroine is reading: the peacocks and the pidavam are right that it rained and wrong that the season has come. The cloud is only emptying its old store, so the thunder is not the promised monsoon. The mutal is negated: the friend says outright that this is not kaar.

thinai_evidence.note: the waiting wife grieving at the season of his promised return

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; இகுளை in line 4 names the addressee

iraicchi.act: the peacocks take a stray cloud's thunder for the season and dance to meet it
iraicchi.sense: the heroine, grieving because she thinks the season of his promise has come and gone unkept, is answering the same false sign

252.reading: The woman tells her friend not to be angry for urging her, 'you are simple indeed', because when the crooked man of the hill country who loosened the armlets on her long rounded arms comes, she tends him with a chastity like a god's, her sweet face unchanged: the worthy feel shame even before praise, so how could they bring themselves to blame when they see him?
252.nuance: She turns a lover's weakness into a rule of the noble: face to face is no place for reproach. She calls him கொடியன் and admits the fault in full before she explains why she will not speak it. The situation, a wife urged to sulk over the man's fault, is marutham's, though the man is of the hills.

thinai_evidence.note: she refuses the sulking her friend urges on her over his fault

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; தோழி in line 6 names the addressee

253.reading: The friend tells the heroine that the men who crossed the high-peaked, crag-ringed hill, where on the slope of rustling tall bamboo travellers on the road sleep in a rock cave reeking of flesh where a tiger has been, are not men who will fail to hear; and if they hear of you lying on the flower bed of loosened threads, your great beauty lost, they will not tarry, even if a great thing is slipping from them.
253.nuance: The comfort is doubled and conditional: they are not the kind who do not hear, and if they hear they will not delay. The road, where travellers sleep in a tiger's flesh-smelling den, shows both how far he is and that he has borne worse than coming home. புலிபுகா உறுத்த in line 6 is hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the hills and she wastes in separation

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; தோழி in line 1 names the addressee

254.reading: The woman tells her friend that the first blossoms of the kongu have come, its soft buds, lovely as breasts, opened on leafless branches loud with swarms of bees; but the message has not come saying he is here: the man who went in desire of bringing back wealth, who in the nights meant for sleep has forgotten sleep, and does not think of the bed of her hair fragrant with resin.
254.nuance: The kongu, flowering on bare branches, keeps its time; the messenger is the sign that fails. She counts what he has forgotten in three things, sleep, her hair as his pillow and the season, all set against the wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone for wealth and she waits past the season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; தோழி in line 3 names the addressee

255.reading: The friend tells the heroine that on the road their beloved took, gone bound by the lovely desire for wealth and meaning to fulfil their duty, the men have seen, at place after place, the great-tusked elephant that gores the cracked-barked trunk of the solid-cored yaa tree on the path, pulls it down with its fierce broad trunk and so relieves the burning hunger of its small-eyed great herd that walks with weary steps.
255.nuance: The elephant feeds not one mate but the whole herd, which matches the men who left to discharge their own obligation (தங்கடன்). The friend's comfort is that a man who watched that at every halt cannot forget whom he is bound to provide for.

thinai_evidence.note: the yaa tree on the dry path is the paalai road

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; தோழி in line 5 names the addressee

iraicchi.act: the tusker strips the yaa tree to ease the hunger of its weary herd
iraicchi.sense: the men who saw it on the road will remember the household they went out to provide for, and come back to it

256.reading: The man says that before he could even say, 'Leaving behind the forest where the stag frisks after feeding with its doe on the soft tendrils of the dark arugu creeper, strung like gems, I will come back when the work is done; can you bear it till then, you with flower earrings?', her eyes would not stay, could not stop weeping their flood of tears, and stood across his chariot's way.
256.nuance: The departure is defeated before it is announced: he has the sentence ready and her eyes answer it first. தேர் விலங்கின, the eyes stood across the chariot, makes tears a barrier on the road. The colophon names no poet.

thinai_evidence.note: the man about to leave for work, and the leaving stopped

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker; the man tells how his going was stopped

iraicchi.act: the stag feeds with its doe and stays in the forest with her
iraicchi.sense: the beasts keep to their mates, which is exactly what the man was proposing to give up

257.reading: The woman tells her friend that the enemy of our love comes every time the man of the roaring hill comes, the hill of jackfruit whose fruit hangs from root, trunk and branch alike as if strung together, low as the drooping thodari; and when he goes it does not go, but stays and fights.
257.nuance: The enemy is not named; since it comes with him and stays after him it is most likely the town's talk or the watch kept on her. The jackfruit loaded on every part is the hill's plenty; a traditional reading takes fruit hanging from the very root as a love too heavy to stay hidden, but the poem draws no correspondence, so it is not tagged as ullurai. Line 2's தொடரி and what it compares are uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the jackfruit hill is kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the jackfruit hanging on root, trunk and branch

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; தோழி in line 6 names the addressee

258.reading: The friend tells the man not to come to their street and not to give his garland: talk has risen, lord, on seeing the flawless fine beauty of this girl wasting, she who is like Arkkadu of Azhisi, father of Chendan whose high-tusked elephant is tied to the marutham at the great Kaveri ford where many bathe, Azhisi, lord of young men with bright swords in rows who live on toddy and the hunt.
258.nuance: Refusing the garland at the street refuses his re-entry. The girl is likened to a chieftain's rich town, so her beauty is a holding like Arkkadu, and its wasting is what the street has seen. Line 1's தாரனின் றாரே divides as தாரல் நின் தாரே; line 5 is compressed.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend bars the straying man from the street

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; பெரும in line 2 names the man

259.reading: The friend tells the dark girl, whose fragrant forehead smells without end like the opened bud of the cool, fragrant kaanthal fed by the waterfalls of the rain-clouded hill, and whose rain-cool eyes are many-petalled, that whether she consents or kills, she herself has measured and knows her own worth: why tell lies that pass for truth? The heart is well disposed toward you.
259.nuance: The friend corners the girl into the truth: she will not let her pretend nothing has happened. ஒல்வை யாயினுங் கொல்வை யாயினும், consent or kill, puts the man's life in the girl's hands, the vocabulary of a suit. Whose heart is good toward her in line 8, the friend's or the man's, is not said.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal of the rainy hill is kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; மாஅயோயே in line 4 names the addressee

260.reading: The friend asks whether he will come: the herons climb the wide sky, the bushes have opened their mouths as striped bees hum, and the shoulders adorned with curled bangles are growing full; will they come back, friend, who crossed the wasteland of thin-stemmed omai trees lying across the way, near the vazhai-covered slopes of the Thondaiyar of generous chariots, whose lordly elephant takes the soil of its foes?
260.nuance: The friend reads three signs at once, sky, bush and body: the shoulders that had wasted are filling out, taken as an omen. The return is still a question (வருவர்கொல்) and the road is hard, so the signs give hope, not news. Line 7, கன்றி லோரா விலங்கிய, does not construe with confidence, and செற்றும் in line 3 may mean the shoulders grow firm or are pressed.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the wasteland and she waits

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives only the speaker; தோழி in line 4 names the addressee

links.note: Kural 1171: the woman asks why her eyes weep, when it was they who showed him to her and brought on the sickness; Kuruntokai 241: she bears her desire, while her eyes, which saw the hill man, weep out of their own intimacy.
links.teaches: The couplet blames the eyes as the cause that now complains, while the poem excuses them as loyal intimates of the man, so the same weeping eyes can be charged as culprits or honoured as the part of her that keeps faith with what it saw.

links.note: Kural 1207: she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns; Kuruntokai 243: she resolves not to think of the shore lord so that her eyes may sleep.
links.teaches: The poem tries the remedy the couplet says is impossible, a vow not to remember, and the very need to vow it confirms the couplet: remembering keeps her awake and forgetting cannot be chosen, only resolved.

links.note: Kural 1188: people say she has grown pale, and no one says he left her; Kuruntokai 245: worse than her lost beauty would be his unkindness becoming known to many.
links.teaches: On the plain reading the two women want opposite things from the town: the couplet's woman resents that the blame falls on her body and not on him, the poem's woman dreads exactly that blame reaching him, so the lover can either demand that the fault be named or shield it at her own cost.

links.note: Kural 791: nothing is as ruinous as befriending without inquiry, for once formed a friendship cannot be left; Kuruntokai 247: the friend says she knew then that the man's friendship is flawless, fruitful, righteous and a raft for kin.
links.teaches: The Kural's test of friendship is meant to come before the bond, but in secret love the bond comes first, so the friend's knowing it to be flawless arrives after the fact and has to argue, in the Kural's own terms of fruit and kin, that the inquiry would have passed.

links.note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my home and feast the evening; Kuruntokai 250: the man tells his charioteer to drive the swift horses before evening comes, for her distress.
links.teaches: The couplet names evening as the feast the returning man looks to; the poem shows why it is a deadline as well as a reward: evening is the hour the stag is with its mate and the hour she suffers most alone, so he must beat it.

links.note: Kuruntokai 65: the stag that drank the clear water among the hard pebbles frisks with its sweet mate, as if mocking the woman who waits; Kuruntokai 250: the stag that drank the water of the pebbled hollow frisks with its mate as the man hurries home.
links.teaches: The anthology uses one sight from both ends of the separation: to the waiting woman the frisking pair is a taunt, to the returning man it is a spur, so the same iraicchi accuses the absence on one side and hastens its end on the other.

links.note: Kuruntokai 66: the friend calls the konrai foolish for taking a stray rain for the season and flowering; Kuruntokai 251: the friend calls the peacocks foolish for dancing to a stray cloud's thunder, and explains the cloud is only emptying its old water.
links.teaches: Together they show the friend's consolation as an argument about evidence, not a denial of rain: in 66 the flowers misread the rain, in 251 the cloud's thunder is given a cause of its own, so the friend separates rain from season, the very distinction the man's promise rests on.

links.note: Kural 1286: when she sees him she sees no fault, when she does not see him she sees only faults; Kuruntokai 252: urged by her friend to reproach him, she says the worthy cannot speak blame to a face.
links.teaches: The couplet presents her silence before him as a blindness of love; the poem's woman sees the fault plainly and calls him crooked, yet keeps silent by a rule of the noble, so the same silence can be read as love's blindness or as chosen restraint.

links.note: Akananuru 59: on the road for wealth an elephant bends a yaa tree so its young mate can eat, yet the man forgets her; Kuruntokai 255: on that road the elephant strips the yaa tree to feed its whole hungry herd, and the men went to fulfil their duty.
links.teaches: The same road-sign is turned two ways by the friend: feeding one mate in Akananuru 59 shames the man who forgets his wife, while feeding the whole herd in Kuruntokai 255 matches the man's duty to his household, so the friend can use the elephant to reproach the journey or to justify it.

links.note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Kuruntokai 256: before he could say he would return when the work was done, her weeping eyes blocked his chariot.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the woman's spoken refusal of the promise of a quick return; the poem shows that refusal made without words, before the promise is spoken, and records that it worked: the chariot stopped.

links.note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone her shoulders have lost their fullness and the bangles slip; Kuruntokai 260: the bangled shoulders are filling out again, read with heron and bush as a sign he will return.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the shoulders a record of his absence; the poem reads them forward as an omen of his return, so the body that registers separation is also consulted to foretell its end.

source_issues.issue: TSCII repair at line 6 (தெளி form); text reads as repaired. Line 1 (ஆய மாய்ந்த) and line 4 (மாலைவேல்) divide uncertainly.
Line 1 is repeated verbatim as Kuruntokai 313 line 1; a formulaic opening, not an error.
Colophon gives the friend as speaker, but the poem addresses தோழி; read as the friend addressing the heroine, though the heroine as speaker is also possible.
தாரனின் றாரே is read as தாரல் நின் தாரே; line 5 (அரியலம் புகவி னந்தோட்டு) is obscure.
கன்றி லோரா விலங்கிய does not construe with confidence.
